title: ☢️ Atomic Physics Lab
description: Welcome to the Atomic Physics Lab! You are a Grade 10 student selected as junior researcher at the school's atomic physics center. Over 14 weeks, dive into the subatomic world — explore Bohr's atomic model, understand radioactive decay, distinguish alpha, beta, and gamma radiation, calculate half-lives, and debate the ethics of nuclear energy. Can you unlock the secrets of the atom and earn the title of Nuclear Physicist?
subject: physics
how_to_play: You are a Grade 10 student exploring atomic physics over a 14-week research program.
Each week presents an atomic physics challenge with choices affecting your knowledge, research quality, and ethics standing.
Watch your dashboard — your Research Stations (Atomic Models, Radiation Lab, Nuclear Reactions, Detection, Ethics Board) are interconnected.
NPCs like Dr. Curie (teacher), Rohan (analytical partner), and Ananya (ethical thinker) react to your decisions.
Random events like radiation safety drills and breakthrough discoveries will test your adaptability.
Keep your Radiation Safety high — careless handling of radioactive concepts has real consequences!
learning_objectives: Describe atomic structure using Bohr's model with energy levels
Distinguish between alpha, beta, and gamma radiation and their properties
Understand radioactive decay and calculate half-life problems
Explain nuclear fission and fusion reactions with mass-energy equivalence
Evaluate the benefits and risks of nuclear energy and radiation applications
Develop critical thinking about ethical dimensions of nuclear science
cultural_context: Advanced school physics research center, nuclear science exploration, ethical scientific inquiry

behaviors.message: Radiation safety is not optional! Even though we use simulations and low-level sources, the habits you form now matter. Marie Curie herself suffered from radiation exposure. Take this seriously.
Nuclear science carries enormous ethical weight. From Hiroshima to Chernobyl, the consequences of irresponsible science are devastating. I expect deeper ethical reflection from you.
Your understanding of atomic physics is matched by your ethical awareness. This combination makes you a responsible scientist. I am nominating you for the Young Scientist Award!
Your atomic models and research quality are extraordinary! You think like a physicist — questioning assumptions, building models, testing predictions. I see a future scientist in you!
Our half-life data is robust! I plotted the decay curve and it fits an exponential perfectly. The calculated half-life matches the accepted value within 3%. Solid science!
We cannot draw conclusions without data! Half-life calculations need at least 8 data points to be meaningful. Let us run more decay simulations.
I noticed something — if we plot ln(N) vs time, we should get a straight line with slope = -λ. From λ we can calculate half-life as t½ = 0.693/λ. Let us verify!
Our team works like a real research group! Ananya handles ethics review, I analyze data, and you design experiments. This is professional-level collaboration.
I appreciate how we are considering the human impact of nuclear science. From cancer treatment to Fukushima, every discovery has consequences. Responsible science is good science.

We cannot just study nuclear physics without thinking about its implications! The atomic bomb, nuclear waste, radiation exposure — these are not abstract problems. People's lives depend on ethical scientists.
Now that we understand fission and fusion, we should debate: is nuclear energy worth the risks? I have been researching both sides and the arguments are compelling.
Nuclear science requires diverse perspectives! If we only think about the physics and ignore the human side, we are no better than the scientists who built weapons without questioning.

rounds.situation: Dr. Curie projects a giant atom on the screen — a tiny dense nucleus surrounded by electron clouds. 'Everything you see, touch, and are — is made of atoms,' she says. 'Today we explore atomic structure: protons, neutrons, electrons, and the forces that hold them together. This is where physics meets chemistry.'
rounds.goal: Understand basic atomic structure and the subatomic particles.
rounds.coaching_moment: Delayed gratification: Atomic structure is the foundation of nuclear physics. Master this, and fission and fusion will make intuitive sense.
rounds.reflection_prompt: If the nucleus were the size of a marble, how far away would the electrons be? What does this tell us about atoms?
rounds.image_prompt: Large atomic model projection showing nucleus with protons and neutrons, electron orbits, Grade 10 students in modern physics lab, periodic table on wall

choices.label: A. An atom has a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus containing protons and neutrons, with electrons orbiting in energy levels. Most of the atom is empty space
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Rutherford's gold foil experiment (1911) revealed that the atom is mostly empty space with a tiny, dense, positive nucleus (diameter ~10⁻¹⁵ m vs atom ~10⁻¹⁰ m). The nucleus contains protons (+1 charge) and neutrons (neutral), while electrons (-1 charge) orbit in energy levels. The nucleus is 100,000 times smaller than the atom but contains 99.9% of its mass.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: B. Protons and electrons are found inside the nucleus, while neutrons orbit outside — this is why the nucleus has both positive and negative charges
choices.feedback: 💡 Electrons are NOT inside the nucleus! The nucleus contains only protons and neutrons (collectively called nucleons). Electrons orbit the nucleus in energy levels. The nuclear force (strong force) holds protons and neutrons together against electromagnetic repulsion. If electrons were in the nucleus, atoms would not have the chemical properties we observe.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Flexibility in your thinking helps you handle change effectively.

choices.label: C. The number of neutrons in an atom is always equal to the number of protons, which is why atoms are electrically neutral
choices.feedback: 💡 Two errors! (1) Neutrons don't equal protons for most elements — only hydrogen-1 and helium-4 are exceptions. Carbon-12 has 6 protons and 6 neutrons, but Carbon-14 has 6 protons and 8 neutrons. (2) Atoms are neutral because the number of electrons equals the number of protons (not neutrons). Neutrons have no charge and don't affect electrical neutrality.

skill_explanation.resilience: Facing challenges head-on strengthens your resilience over time.

choices.label: D. In Rutherford's gold foil experiment, most alpha particles bounced straight back, proving that the atom is densely packed with matter throughout
choices.feedback: 💡 Most alpha particles passed straight through! Only about 1 in 8,000 bounced back at large angles. This proved that the atom is mostly empty space with a tiny, dense nucleus. If the atom were densely packed (like Thomson's plum pudding model), all alpha particles would deflect significantly. The rare large deflections indicated a concentrated positive charge in a very small region.

skill_explanation.empathy: Valuing others' experiences alongside your own shows empathetic thinking.

rounds.situation: Dr. Curie draws Bohr's model: electrons orbiting the nucleus in fixed energy levels. 'Niels Bohr showed that electrons can only exist at specific energy levels — like steps on a staircase, not a ramp,' she explains. 'When electrons jump between levels, they absorb or emit specific amounts of energy — that is why neon lights glow specific colors!'
rounds.goal: Understand Bohr's model, energy levels, and electron transitions.
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: Bohr's model explains atomic spectra — the 'fingerprints' of elements. This connects atomic structure to observable light.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why do different elements produce different colored flames when heated? How does Bohr's model explain this?
rounds.image_prompt: Bohr model diagram with energy levels labeled K/L/M/N, electron jumping between levels emitting a photon, colorful spectral lines, physics lab whiteboard

choices.label: A. In Bohr's model, electrons orbit the nucleus in fixed energy levels. They can only jump between levels by absorbing or emitting a photon with energy exactly equal to the level difference
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Bohr's key postulate: electrons occupy discrete energy levels (n = 1, 2, 3...). Transitions between levels require absorbing (jumping up) or emitting (jumping down) a photon of specific energy: E_photon = E_higher - E_lower = hf. This explains why atoms emit line spectra (discrete colors), not continuous spectra. Each element has unique energy level spacings, producing unique spectral lines.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: B. In Bohr's model, electrons can orbit at any distance from the nucleus, smoothly spiraling inward as they lose energy through radiation
choices.feedback: 💡 This describes exactly what Bohr's model was designed to prevent! In classical physics, orbiting electrons would continuously radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus (atom collapse). Bohr proposed that electrons can ONLY exist in specific, quantized orbits. They don't radiate while in these orbits, and can only change orbits through discrete quantum jumps.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Adjusting your approach when conditions change shows flexibility.

choices.label: C. An electron in the ground state (n=1) has the highest energy because it is closest to the nucleus and experiences the strongest attraction
choices.feedback: 💡 The ground state has the LOWEST (most negative) energy! Stronger attraction means the electron is more tightly bound, which corresponds to lower potential energy. Higher orbits (n=2, 3...) have higher energy. It's like a ball in a valley vs on a hill — the ball in the valley has less potential energy but is in a more stable position. To move an electron to a higher level, you must ADD energy.

skill_explanation.resilience: Pushing through difficulty builds mental strength.

choices.label: D. The line spectrum of hydrogen has only one spectral line because hydrogen has only one electron that can make one transition
choices.feedback: 💡 Hydrogen produces many spectral lines! Even though it has one electron, that electron can be excited to many different energy levels (n=2, 3, 4...) and then cascade down through various transitions. Each transition produces a different wavelength. The Balmer series alone (transitions to n=2) has visible lines at 656 nm (red), 486 nm (blue-green), 434 nm (blue), and more.

skill_explanation.empathy: Considering how others feel shows emotional intelligence.

rounds.situation: Dr. Curie brings out a Geiger counter and holds it near a small mineral sample. Click-click-click-click! 'That clicking sound is radioactive decay — atoms spontaneously breaking apart!' she explains. 'Henri Becquerel discovered this by accident in 1896, and Marie Curie spent her life studying it. Today, you discover the three types of radiation.'
rounds.goal: Understand radioactivity and distinguish between alpha, beta, and gamma radiation.
rounds.coaching_moment: Risk tolerance: Radioactivity was discovered through curiosity and careful observation. The best scientists take calculated risks while maintaining safety.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why are some atoms radioactive while others are stable? What makes a nucleus unstable?
rounds.image_prompt: Geiger counter clicking near a mineral sample, three paths showing alpha/beta/gamma radiation between magnetic field poles, physics lab, students observing

choices.label: A. Alpha particles have the highest ionizing power but the lowest penetrating power — they are stopped by a sheet of paper. Gamma rays have the lowest ionizing power but the highest penetrating power
choices.learning_concept: Properties of Alpha, Beta, Gamma Radiation
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Ionizing power and penetrating power are inversely related. Alpha particles (²He⁴) are heavy and highly charged (+2), so they ionize intensely but lose energy quickly — stopped by paper or skin. Beta particles (electrons) are lighter — stopped by aluminium. Gamma rays (photons) are massless and uncharged — they penetrate through centimetres of lead. More mass/charge = more ionization but less penetration.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: B. Gamma rays are the most dangerous radiation because they have the highest ionizing power — they ionize every atom they pass through
choices.feedback: 💡 Gamma rays have the LOWEST ionizing power, not the highest! Alpha particles are the strongest ionizers. Gamma rays are dangerous because of their high penetrating power — they can pass through the body, damaging internal organs. Alpha particles are harmless externally (stopped by skin) but extremely dangerous if ingested or inhaled because they ionize tissue intensely at close range.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Being open to new information and changing course builds adaptability.

choices.label: C. Beta particles are positively charged helium nuclei that are deflected by electric and magnetic fields toward the negative plate
choices.feedback: 💡 You've confused alpha and beta! Alpha particles are helium nuclei (2 protons + 2 neutrons, charge +2), deflected toward the negative plate. Beta particles are high-speed electrons (charge -1), deflected toward the positive plate. Beta particles are much lighter and have the opposite charge to alpha particles. Gamma rays, being uncharged photons, pass through undeflected.

skill_explanation.resilience: Choosing to persist when things get hard develops resilience.

choices.label: D. Radioactive decay is a chemical reaction that can be speeded up by increasing temperature or using a catalyst, just like other chemical reactions
choices.feedback: 💡 Radioactive decay is a NUCLEAR process, not a chemical reaction! It involves changes in the nucleus (protons/neutrons), while chemical reactions only involve outer electrons. Nuclear decay is completely unaffected by temperature, pressure, catalysts, or any external conditions. The rate depends only on the nuclear properties of the isotope. This is why radioactive waste remains dangerous for thousands of years.

skill_explanation.empathy: Taking others' perspectives into account builds empathy.

rounds.situation: Dr. Curie writes on the board: 'Half-life = time for half the radioactive atoms to decay.' She hands out 100 dice to each team. 'Roll them all. Remove every die showing a 6. Count what remains. Repeat. You are simulating radioactive decay!' The exercise brilliantly demonstrates exponential decay with dice.
rounds.goal: Understand half-life through simulation and mathematical analysis.
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: Half-life is a probability concept — you cannot predict which atom will decay, only what fraction will. Embracing uncertainty is key to modern physics.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Carbon-14 has a half-life of 5,730 years. If a fossil has 25% of its original C-14, how old is it?
rounds.image_prompt: Students rolling 100 dice on lab tables, removing sixes, plotting decay curve on graph paper, exponential decay equation on whiteboard, excited learning

choices.label: A. A radioactive sample with half-life 6 hours starts with 800 g. After 18 hours (3 half-lives): 800→400→200→100 g remains, so 700 g has decayed
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Number of half-lives = 18/6 = 3. After each half-life, half the remaining atoms decay: 800→400 (1st)→200 (2nd)→100 g (3rd). Amount decayed = 800 - 100 = 700 g. The general formula is: remaining = initial × (½)^n, where n = number of half-lives. This exponential decay is fundamental to nuclear physics and has no dependence on external conditions.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: B. After one half-life, a 100 g sample becomes 50 g. After two half-lives, it becomes 0 g because the second half-life removes the remaining 50 g
choices.feedback: 💡 Each half-life removes half of what REMAINS, not half of the original! After 1 half-life: 100→50 g. After 2 half-lives: 50→25 g (not 0). After 3: 25→12.5 g. The sample never reaches exactly 0 g — it approaches zero asymptotically. This is exponential decay: each half-life halves the current amount. Mathematically, the sample would take infinite time to fully decay.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Pivoting your strategy when needed is a sign of adaptive thinking.

choices.label: C. The half-life of a radioactive substance decreases as the sample gets smaller because fewer atoms means fewer decays per second
choices.feedback: 💡 Half-life is CONSTANT — it never changes regardless of sample size! While the decay rate (number of decays per second) does decrease with fewer atoms, the fraction that decays per unit time stays the same. Half-life is an intrinsic property of the isotope. Carbon-14's half-life is 5,730 years whether you have 1 gram or 1 ton.

skill_explanation.resilience: Learning from setbacks rather than giving up shows resilience.

choices.label: D. If an isotope has a half-life of 10 days, then after 10 days exactly half the atoms will have decayed and the other half will be stable non-radioactive atoms
choices.feedback: 💡 The undecayed atoms are NOT stable — they are still radioactive! After one half-life, the remaining 50% are the same radioactive isotope, still subject to the same probability of decay. They will continue to decay with the same half-life. The decayed atoms transform into daughter nuclei (which may be stable or may themselves be radioactive, forming a decay chain).

skill_explanation.empathy: Understanding the impact on people around you shows care for others.

rounds.situation: Dr. Curie shows an animation of a uranium-235 nucleus being hit by a neutron. It wobbles, elongates, and splits into two smaller nuclei plus more neutrons and enormous energy! 'This is nuclear fission — splitting the atom,' she says. 'It powers nuclear reactors AND nuclear bombs. The same physics, two very different applications.'
rounds.goal: Understand nuclear fission, chain reactions, and E = mc².
rounds.coaching_moment: Ethical reasoning: Fission can generate clean electricity OR destroy cities. The same knowledge can be used for good or harm. Scientists bear responsibility for how their work is applied.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Einstein's E = mc² shows that a tiny mass converts to enormous energy. If 1 gram of matter were fully converted to energy, how much energy would that be?
rounds.image_prompt: Uranium-235 nucleus splitting after neutron impact, two daughter nuclei flying apart with neutrons and energy, chain reaction diagram, dramatic physics visualization

choices.label: A. In nuclear fission, a heavy nucleus like U-235 splits into two lighter nuclei when hit by a slow neutron, releasing enormous energy and 2-3 more neutrons that can cause a chain reaction
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Fission of U-235: a slow (thermal) neutron is absorbed, making U-236, which is unstable and splits into two fragments (e.g., Ba-141 + Kr-92) plus 2-3 neutrons and ~200 MeV of energy. The released neutrons can trigger fission in other U-235 atoms, creating a chain reaction. This is the basis of nuclear power plants and atomic bombs.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: B. Nuclear fission produces energy by combining light nuclei into heavier ones — the Sun uses fission to generate its energy
choices.feedback: 💡 You've described nuclear FUSION, not fission! Fission = splitting heavy nuclei (like uranium). Fusion = combining light nuclei (like hydrogen). The Sun uses fusion (combining hydrogen into helium). Both processes release energy because the products have less mass than the reactants — the 'missing' mass is converted to energy via E = mc².

skill_explanation.adaptability: Responding to unexpected situations with creativity shows adaptability.

choices.label: C. In a nuclear chain reaction, each fission event produces exactly one neutron, which triggers exactly one more fission, making the reaction self-sustaining
choices.feedback: 💡 Each fission produces 2-3 neutrons, not just one! This multiplication is what makes chain reactions possible but also potentially dangerous. In a nuclear reactor, control rods absorb excess neutrons to maintain exactly 1 neutron per fission (critical state). In a bomb, the reaction is uncontrolled — each fission triggers multiple fissions, causing exponential growth and a massive explosion.

skill_explanation.resilience: Staying focused under pressure builds your ability to bounce back.

choices.label: D. Nuclear fission can occur with any element — iron, gold, and carbon can all undergo fission if struck by a neutron with enough energy
choices.feedback: 💡 Only very heavy nuclei (like U-235, U-238, Pu-239) can undergo fission! These nuclei are so large that the strong nuclear force barely holds them together, making them susceptible to splitting. Lighter elements like iron, gold, and carbon have very stable nuclei with high binding energy per nucleon — they resist fission. Iron-56 is actually the most stable nucleus.

skill_explanation.empathy: Listening to different viewpoints strengthens your empathy skills.

rounds.round_title: Week 6: Nuclear Fusion — Power of the Stars
rounds.situation: Dr. Curie shows an image of the Sun. 'Every second, the Sun fuses 600 million tons of hydrogen into helium, releasing energy that lights our entire solar system,' she says. 'Fusion is the opposite of fission — small nuclei combine. It produces no radioactive waste and uses hydrogen from water. It is the holy grail of energy — but incredibly hard to achieve on Earth.'
rounds.goal: Understand nuclear fusion, stellar nucleosynthesis, and the quest for fusion energy.
rounds.coaching_moment: Resilience: Scientists have been trying to achieve controlled fusion for 70 years. It is the hardest engineering challenge ever attempted. Persistence defines progress.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why is it so difficult to make two hydrogen nuclei fuse? What conditions are needed to overcome their electrical repulsion?
rounds.image_prompt: Diagram of hydrogen fusion into helium inside the Sun, proton-proton chain, massive energy release, comparison of fusion vs fission, stellar core visualization

choices.label: A. Nuclear fusion combines light nuclei (like hydrogen isotopes) at extremely high temperatures (~10⁷ K) to form heavier nuclei, releasing energy because the products have higher binding energy per nucleon
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Fusion requires extreme temperatures to overcome the electrostatic repulsion between positively charged nuclei. In the Sun, hydrogen fuses to helium: 4¹H → ⁴He + 2 positrons + 2 neutrinos + energy. The energy comes from mass loss (the helium is lighter than 4 hydrogen atoms). Fusion releases more energy per unit mass than fission and produces no radioactive waste.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: B. Nuclear fusion occurs easily at room temperature because light nuclei naturally attract each other due to the strong nuclear force
choices.feedback: 💡 Fusion requires millions of degrees! At room temperature, the electromagnetic repulsion between positive nuclei keeps them far apart. The strong nuclear force only acts at extremely short range (~10⁻¹⁵ m). Nuclei must be moving fast enough (high temperature) to overcome this 'Coulomb barrier.' This is why achieving controlled fusion on Earth is so technically challenging.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Flexibility in your thinking helps you handle change effectively.

choices.label: C. Stars like our Sun generate energy through nuclear fission of heavy elements in their core, which is why stars eventually run out of fuel and die
choices.feedback: 💡 Stars use FUSION, not fission! The Sun fuses hydrogen into helium in its core at ~15 million K. Stars do run out of fuel — but it's fusion fuel (hydrogen), not fission fuel. After hydrogen is exhausted, massive stars fuse helium into carbon, then carbon into heavier elements, up to iron. Beyond iron, fusion requires energy instead of releasing it, leading to the star's death.

skill_explanation.resilience: Facing challenges head-on strengthens your resilience over time.

choices.label: D. Fusion reactions produce more radioactive waste than fission reactions because the extreme temperatures create unstable isotopes as byproducts
choices.feedback: 💡 Fusion produces far LESS radioactive waste than fission! The main fusion product (helium) is completely non-radioactive and non-toxic. Fission produces highly radioactive waste products that remain dangerous for thousands of years. This is one of the biggest advantages of fusion power — if we can achieve controlled fusion, it would be cleaner and safer than fission.

skill_explanation.empathy: Valuing others' experiences alongside your own shows empathetic thinking.

rounds.situation: Dr. Curie sets up three radiation detection devices: a Geiger-Muller counter (click-click), a cloud chamber (visible tracks!), and a scintillation counter. 'You cannot see, hear, or feel radiation,' she says. 'These instruments are our eyes into the invisible atomic world. Today you learn to detect and measure what your senses cannot.'
rounds.goal: Master radiation detection methods and measurement techniques.
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: Choosing the right detection method for the right situation is critical. A Geiger counter detects presence; a scintillation counter measures energy.
rounds.reflection_prompt: In a cloud chamber, alpha particles leave thick short tracks while beta particles leave thin long tracks. Why do they look so different?
rounds.image_prompt: Cloud chamber showing particle tracks, Geiger counter clicking, scintillation counter on bench, students observing vapor trails of alpha particles, dark physics lab

choices.label: A. A Geiger-Muller counter detects radiation by measuring ionization in a gas-filled tube — each radiation particle ionizes gas atoms, creating a brief pulse of current that is counted
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ A Geiger counter has a gas-filled tube with a thin window. When radiation enters, it ionizes gas atoms, creating free electrons that are attracted to a central anode. This triggers a cascade of ionizations (avalanche), producing a measurable current pulse. Each pulse = one detected particle. The characteristic clicking sound indicates individual radiation events. It's simple, portable, and effective for alpha, beta, and gamma detection.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: B. A Geiger counter directly measures the energy of radiation — the louder the click, the more energetic the radiation particle
choices.feedback: 💡 A Geiger counter CANNOT measure radiation energy! It only counts the number of radiation events (particles detected). Each pulse is the same size regardless of the radiation's energy — the avalanche effect saturates the response. For energy measurement, you need a scintillation counter or semiconductor detector. The Geiger counter tells you how much radiation, not how energetic each particle is.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Adjusting your approach when conditions change shows flexibility.

choices.label: C. Background radiation is entirely caused by human activities like nuclear power plants and medical X-rays — there is no natural source of radiation
choices.feedback: 💡 Most background radiation is NATURAL! Sources include: cosmic rays from space, radon gas from rocks/soil (the largest natural source), radioactive elements in food (potassium-40 in bananas), and radioactive minerals in the ground. Only about 15-20% of background radiation comes from human activities (medical X-rays, nuclear industry). Natural radiation has existed since Earth formed.

skill_explanation.resilience: Pushing through difficulty builds mental strength.

choices.label: D. Cloud chambers detect radiation by freezing water droplets around radiation particles — colder chambers detect more types of radiation
choices.feedback: 💡 Cloud chambers use supersaturated vapor, not freezing! The chamber contains vapor just below its condensation point. When a radiation particle passes through, it ionizes gas molecules along its path. These ions act as condensation nuclei, and tiny droplets form along the track, making the particle's path visible. Alpha particles leave thick, short tracks; beta particles leave thin, long tracks; gamma rays leave very faint, scattered tracks.

skill_explanation.empathy: Considering how others feel shows emotional intelligence.

rounds.situation: Dr. Curie shows images: cancer treatment with gamma rays, smoke detectors using americium-241, food preservation by irradiation, PET scans using positron-emitting isotopes. 'Radiation saves millions of lives every year,' she says. 'The same physics that can harm also heals. Today we explore the many beneficial applications of radioactivity.'
rounds.goal: Understand medical, industrial, and agricultural applications of radiation.
rounds.coaching_moment: Empathy: Nuclear medicine saves millions of lives yearly. Understanding both risks and benefits requires balanced, compassionate thinking.
rounds.reflection_prompt: How does radiotherapy use gamma rays to kill cancer cells while minimizing damage to healthy tissue?
rounds.image_prompt: Medical radiation therapy machine treating patient, smoke detector cross-section showing americium source, PET scan brain image, food irradiation facility, collage of applications

choices.label: A. Carbon-14 dating works because living organisms constantly absorb C-14 from the atmosphere, but after death C-14 decays with a half-life of 5,730 years. Measuring remaining C-14 reveals the age
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ While alive, organisms maintain the same C-14/C-12 ratio as the atmosphere through respiration/eating. After death, C-14 decays without being replaced. By comparing the remaining C-14 to the expected amount, scientists calculate the time since death. After 5,730 years, half the C-14 has decayed. Carbon dating is reliable up to ~50,000 years and has revolutionized archaeology.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: B. Radioactive tracers in medicine work by killing cancer cells — doctors inject radioactive material that targets and destroys tumors
choices.feedback: 💡 Tracers are for DIAGNOSIS, not treatment! A small amount of a radioactive isotope (like Technetium-99m) is injected, and a gamma camera detects where it accumulates. This reveals organ function, blood flow, and abnormalities without surgery. The radiation dose is minimal. Cancer TREATMENT uses radiotherapy — focused high-dose radiation — which is a completely different application from tracing.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Being open to new information and changing course builds adaptability.

choices.label: C. Food irradiation makes food radioactive, which is why irradiated food glows and must be labeled as radioactive
choices.feedback: 💡 Irradiated food does NOT become radioactive! Gamma rays from Cobalt-60 kill bacteria and parasites by damaging their DNA, but the food itself does not become radioactive — just as you don't become radioactive after an X-ray. The radiation passes through and is absorbed, but it doesn't make the food emit radiation. Food irradiation is approved as safe by WHO, FDA, and IAEA.

skill_explanation.resilience: Choosing to persist when things get hard develops resilience.

choices.label: D. Smoke detectors use gamma radiation to detect smoke particles — the gamma rays are blocked by smoke, triggering the alarm
choices.feedback: 💡 Smoke detectors use ALPHA radiation (from Americium-241), not gamma! Alpha particles ionize air between two plates, creating a small current. When smoke enters, the smoke particles absorb alpha particles (which have very low penetrating power), reducing the current. The drop in current triggers the alarm. Gamma rays would pass right through smoke without being affected.

skill_explanation.empathy: Taking others' perspectives into account builds empathy.

rounds.round_title: Week 9: Nuclear Power — Promise and Peril
rounds.situation: Dr. Curie projects two images side by side: a nuclear power plant providing clean electricity to a city, and the abandoned Chernobyl reactor. 'Nuclear power produces no CO₂ and can provide baseload electricity for millions,' she says. 'But accidents — however rare — have devastating consequences. Today, we examine both sides with scientific rigor.'
rounds.goal: Evaluate nuclear power's benefits and risks with scientific evidence.
rounds.coaching_moment: Ethical reasoning: Complex problems rarely have simple answers. Nuclear power requires weighing climate benefits against accident risks and waste challenges.
rounds.reflection_prompt: France generates 70% of its electricity from nuclear power with very low carbon emissions. Should other countries follow this model? Why or why not?
rounds.image_prompt: Split image: clean nuclear power plant with cooling towers on one side, abandoned Chernobyl reactor on the other, students debating in middle, evidence posters on walls

choices.label: A. In a nuclear reactor, control rods (made of boron or cadmium) absorb excess neutrons to maintain a controlled chain reaction. Removing rods speeds up the reaction; inserting them slows it down
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Control rods are the 'brake pedal' of a nuclear reactor. Boron and cadmium are excellent neutron absorbers. When fully inserted, they absorb most neutrons, stopping the chain reaction (shutdown). Partially withdrawn, they maintain exactly 1 neutron per fission event (criticality). A moderator (water/graphite) slows neutrons down because slow neutrons are more likely to cause fission in U-235.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: B. Nuclear reactors can explode like atomic bombs if the control rods fail, which is why nuclear power is extremely dangerous
choices.feedback: 💡 A nuclear reactor CANNOT explode like an atomic bomb! Reactor fuel is only 3-5% U-235 (bombs need >80%). If control fails, the reactor can overheat and melt down (as in Chernobyl/Fukushima), causing radiation release, but not a nuclear explosion. A bomb requires supercritical mass of highly enriched uranium or plutonium with precise implosion — conditions impossible in a reactor.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Pivoting your strategy when needed is a sign of adaptive thinking.

choices.label: C. The moderator in a nuclear reactor speeds up neutrons because faster neutrons are more likely to cause fission in uranium-235
choices.feedback: 💡 The moderator SLOWS DOWN neutrons! Fast neutrons released by fission are less likely to be captured by U-235. The moderator (water, heavy water, or graphite) slows them to thermal speeds through collisions, increasing the probability of causing another fission event. This 'thermal neutron' approach is why most reactors are called thermal reactors. Faster is not better for sustaining fission.

skill_explanation.resilience: Learning from setbacks rather than giving up shows resilience.

choices.label: D. Nuclear power plants release large amounts of greenhouse gases during operation, making them as polluting as coal power plants
choices.feedback: 💡 Nuclear power plants produce virtually ZERO greenhouse gases during operation! The fission process releases energy without combustion — no CO₂, SO₂, or particulates. The 'steam' from cooling towers is just water vapor. Nuclear has one of the lowest lifecycle carbon footprints of any energy source. The main environmental concern is radioactive waste disposal, not greenhouse gas emissions.

skill_explanation.empathy: Understanding the impact on people around you shows care for others.

rounds.situation: Dr. Curie writes three versions of carbon on the board: C-12 (stable, 6p+6n), C-13 (stable, 6p+7n), C-14 (radioactive, 6p+8n). 'Same element, different neutron numbers — isotopes!' she explains. 'Isotopes are everywhere: in medicine, archaeology, forensics, and even the food you eat. Understanding isotopes is understanding the diversity of matter itself.'
rounds.goal: Understand isotopes, their notation, and their diverse applications.
rounds.coaching_moment: Adaptability: The same element can have wildly different properties depending on its isotope. Flexibility in thinking about atoms is essential.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Deuterium (hydrogen-2) is used in nuclear fusion research. How does having one extra neutron change hydrogen's properties so dramatically?
rounds.image_prompt: Three carbon isotope models (C-12, C-13, C-14) side by side showing different neutron numbers, isotope notation on board, periodic table with isotope data, modern lab

choices.label: A. Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same atomic number (protons) but different mass numbers (different neutrons). Carbon-12 and Carbon-14 both have 6 protons but 6 and 8 neutrons respectively
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Isotopes have: same atomic number Z (same element, same chemistry), different mass number A (different neutrons). Carbon-12: 6p + 6n = 12. Carbon-14: 6p + 8n = 14. Both are carbon (6 protons), but C-14 is radioactive (unstable) while C-12 is stable. Many elements have stable and radioactive isotopes — hydrogen has 3 isotopes: protium (H-1), deuterium (H-2), and tritium (H-3, radioactive).

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: B. Isotopes of an element have different chemical properties because the extra neutrons change how the electrons bond with other atoms
choices.feedback: 💡 Isotopes have virtually identical chemical properties! Chemical behavior depends on the number and arrangement of electrons, which is determined by the number of protons (atomic number). Since isotopes have the same number of protons, they have the same electrons and the same chemistry. Neutrons affect only the mass and nuclear stability, not chemical bonding.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Responding to unexpected situations with creativity shows adaptability.

choices.label: C. All isotopes are radioactive because having different numbers of neutrons makes the nucleus unstable
choices.feedback: 💡 Most isotopes are STABLE! For example, Carbon-12 and Carbon-13 are both stable isotopes. Only Carbon-14 is radioactive. An isotope is radioactive only if its neutron-to-proton ratio falls outside the 'band of stability.' Most elements have several stable isotopes and a few radioactive ones. Tin has the most stable isotopes (10!) while some elements like technetium have none.

skill_explanation.resilience: Staying focused under pressure builds your ability to bounce back.

choices.label: D. The mass number of an isotope is the number of protons in the nucleus, while the atomic number is the total number of protons and neutrons
choices.feedback: 💡 You have them switched! Atomic number (Z) = number of protons (defines the element). Mass number (A) = protons + neutrons (total nucleons). For Carbon-14: Z = 6 (protons), A = 14 (6 protons + 8 neutrons). The atomic number is always the smaller number. This is a common mix-up — remember: Atomic = proton count, Mass = total nucleon count.

skill_explanation.empathy: Listening to different viewpoints strengthens your empathy skills.

rounds.situation: Dr. Curie writes a nuclear equation on the board: ²³⁵U + ¹n → ¹⁴¹Ba + ⁹²Kr + 3¹n + Energy. 'In every nuclear reaction, mass number and atomic number are conserved,' she says. 'Today you will balance nuclear equations and predict the products of decay and fission reactions.'
rounds.goal: Master nuclear equation balancing and conservation laws in nuclear reactions.
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: Conservation laws are the most powerful tools in physics. If mass number and charge are conserved, you can predict unknown products.
rounds.reflection_prompt: When radium-226 undergoes alpha decay, what element is produced? How do you determine this using conservation laws?
rounds.image_prompt: Nuclear equations on whiteboard showing balanced mass numbers and atomic numbers, student solving decay equations, periodic table reference, physics lab

choices.label: A. In alpha decay, the mass number decreases by 4 and the atomic number decreases by 2. For example: ²³⁸U → ²³⁴Th + ⁴He (alpha particle)
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ In alpha decay, the nucleus emits an alpha particle (⁴₂He — 2 protons + 2 neutrons). So: mass number A decreases by 4, atomic number Z decreases by 2. Uranium-238 (Z=92) → Thorium-234 (Z=90) + alpha particle. Both mass number and atomic number are conserved on both sides: 238 = 234 + 4, and 92 = 90 + 2.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: B. In beta decay, a proton converts to a neutron and emits a positron, so the atomic number decreases by 1 while the mass number stays the same
choices.feedback: 💡 In beta-minus decay (the most common type at this level), a NEUTRON converts to a proton, emitting an electron (beta particle) and an antineutrino. The atomic number INCREASES by 1 (one more proton), while the mass number stays the same. Example: ¹⁴C → ¹⁴N + e⁻. What you described (proton→neutron + positron) is beta-plus decay, which is less common.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Flexibility in your thinking helps you handle change effectively.

choices.label: C. E = mc² means that a small amount of energy can be converted into a large amount of mass because c² is a very large number
choices.feedback: 💡 You have the practical direction reversed! While E = mc² works both ways theoretically, in nuclear reactions a small amount of MASS is converted into a LARGE amount of energy (not the other way). Since c² = 9 × 10¹⁶ m²/s², even a tiny mass loss produces enormous energy. In fission of 1 kg of U-235, only about 1 gram of mass is converted — yet it releases energy equivalent to 20,000 tons of TNT!

skill_explanation.resilience: Facing challenges head-on strengthens your resilience over time.

choices.label: D. In gamma decay, the atomic number and mass number both decrease because the nucleus loses energy by emitting a gamma photon that carries mass
choices.feedback: 💡 In gamma decay, NEITHER atomic number NOR mass number changes! Gamma decay is simply the nucleus releasing excess energy as a gamma ray photon. The photon has zero mass and zero charge, so the nucleus remains the same isotope — just in a lower energy state. Gamma emission often follows alpha or beta decay, as the daughter nucleus releases leftover excitation energy.

skill_explanation.empathy: Valuing others' experiences alongside your own shows empathetic thinking.

rounds.situation: Dr. Curie brings articles about cutting-edge nuclear technology: small modular reactors (SMRs), thorium reactors, proton therapy for cancer, and nuclear-powered spacecraft. 'Nuclear science is not just history — it is the future,' she says. 'Today, explore how modern technology is solving old nuclear problems with new approaches.'
rounds.goal: Explore modern advances in nuclear technology and their implications.
rounds.coaching_moment: Resilience: The nuclear industry has learned from past mistakes. New designs are inherently safer. Progress comes from learning from failure, not abandoning the field.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Small modular reactors can be factory-built and are designed to shut down safely without human intervention. How does this address the problems of large traditional reactors?
rounds.image_prompt: Modern small modular reactor design, proton therapy treatment room, nuclear-powered Mars spacecraft concept, thorium fuel cycle diagram, futuristic technology collage

choices.label: A. Nuclear medicine uses Technetium-99m as a tracer because it emits only gamma rays (easily detected externally), has a short half-life (6 hours), and doesn't damage tissue excessively
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Tc-99m is the ideal medical tracer: (1) Emits gamma rays that pass through the body for external detection. (2) Short half-life (6 h) means radiation exposure is brief. (3) No alpha or beta emission means minimal tissue damage. (4) Gamma energy (140 keV) is perfect for gamma camera imaging. Over 80% of diagnostic nuclear medicine procedures use Tc-99m.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: B. For medical tracers, isotopes with very long half-lives (thousands of years) are preferred because they provide a stable, long-lasting signal for doctors to study
choices.feedback: 💡 Long half-lives would be terrible for medical tracers! The patient would remain radioactive for years, accumulating harmful radiation dose. Ideal medical tracers have half-lives of hours to days — long enough to perform the scan, short enough to minimize radiation exposure. Tc-99m (6 hours) is ideal. After 24 hours (~4 half-lives), only about 6% remains active.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Adjusting your approach when conditions change shows flexibility.

choices.label: C. Radiotherapy for cancer uses low-dose, widespread radiation to gently kill cancer cells throughout the entire body
choices.feedback: 💡 Radiotherapy uses HIGH-dose, precisely FOCUSED radiation targeted at the tumor! The goal is to destroy cancer cells while minimizing damage to surrounding healthy tissue. Multiple beams are often aimed from different angles, intersecting at the tumor to concentrate the dose. Widespread low-dose radiation would damage healthy cells throughout the body without effectively killing the tumor.

skill_explanation.resilience: Pushing through difficulty builds mental strength.

choices.label: D. PET scans (Positron Emission Tomography) work by injecting patients with strong magnets that align with the body's natural magnetic field to create images
choices.feedback: 💡 You're confusing PET with MRI! PET uses radioactive tracers that emit positrons (β⁺). When a positron meets an electron, they annihilate and produce two gamma rays traveling in opposite directions. Detectors around the patient identify these gamma ray pairs to pinpoint where the tracer accumulated. MRI is the technique that uses magnetic fields — PET uses nuclear physics.

skill_explanation.empathy: Considering how others feel shows emotional intelligence.

rounds.situation: One week before the showcase! Dr. Curie gives each team freedom to pursue a capstone research project. 'Use everything you have learned — atomic models, radioactivity, nuclear reactions, detection, applications, and ethics. Create something that demonstrates your understanding AND your values as a scientist.'
rounds.goal: Complete a capstone research project integrating all atomic physics knowledge.
rounds.coaching_moment: Creativity: The best projects combine deep knowledge with personal passion. What aspect of nuclear science excites you most?
rounds.reflection_prompt: If you could ask one question to a nuclear physicist, what would it be? What answer would change how you think about the atom?
rounds.image_prompt: Students working on diverse research projects, atomic models, data analysis on laptops, ethics posters, collaborative work, creative physics lab atmosphere

choices.label: A. Nuclear waste is classified into levels: low-level (gloves, tools) stored in near-surface facilities, and high-level (spent fuel rods) stored deep underground in stable geological formations for thousands of years
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Nuclear waste management is a critical challenge. Low-level waste (90% of volume, 1% of radioactivity) includes contaminated clothing and tools — stored in shallow repositories. High-level waste (spent fuel rods) contains highly radioactive fission products and must be isolated for thousands of years. Deep geological repositories in stable rock formations (like Finland's Onkalo facility) are the current solution.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: B. Nuclear waste can be safely disposed of by diluting it in the ocean because the vast volume of water will reduce the radiation to harmless levels
choices.feedback: 💡 Ocean dumping of nuclear waste is banned internationally! Radioactive materials would bioaccumulate through the food chain — plankton absorb it, fish eat plankton, and concentrations increase at each level. Even small amounts entering the marine ecosystem can affect organisms for generations. The London Convention (1993) prohibits all dumping of radioactive waste at sea.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Being open to new information and changing course builds adaptability.

choices.label: C. All nuclear waste becomes harmless after one half-life because half of the radioactivity has gone, and the remaining half is too weak to cause damage
choices.feedback: 💡 After one half-life, the waste is still 50% as radioactive — still extremely dangerous! Most safety standards require waste to decay through about 10 half-lives (to ~0.1% of original activity) before it's considered safe. Plutonium-239 has a half-life of 24,100 years, meaning it takes ~240,000 years to become relatively safe. This is why permanent geological storage is necessary.

skill_explanation.resilience: Choosing to persist when things get hard develops resilience.

choices.label: D. Nuclear power should be completely banned because there is no way to safely handle radioactive materials — all countries with nuclear power have had major accidents
choices.feedback: 💡 This is an extreme position not supported by evidence. While accidents like Chernobyl and Fukushima were serious, most nuclear nations (30+ countries) have operated safely for decades. France generates ~70% of its electricity from nuclear power with an excellent safety record. Nuclear energy produces no greenhouse gases during operation. The debate requires balancing risks (waste, accidents) against benefits (clean energy, reliability).

skill_explanation.empathy: Taking others' perspectives into account builds empathy.

rounds.situation: Showcase day! The lab is transformed into an atomic physics exhibition. Parents, teachers, younger students, and a nuclear medicine doctor are visiting. Atomic models, radiation detectors, and ethics posters fill the room. Dr. Curie says: 'Show the world that you understand both the power and the responsibility of nuclear science.'
rounds.goal: Present your atomic physics research at the final showcase.
rounds.coaching_moment: Resilience: Presenting complex topics like nuclear physics to non-scientists requires clarity and courage. Your ability to explain and inspire matters more than perfection.
rounds.reflection_prompt: What is the most important thing you learned about atomic physics this semester? How will it change how you see the world?
rounds.image_prompt: Atomic physics showcase with students presenting models and experiments, visiting doctor examining projects, parents observing cloud chamber, ethics display, trophy ceremony

choices.label: A. In a nuclear fission reaction, the mass of the products is slightly less than the mass of the reactants. This 'mass defect' is converted to energy via E = mc², releasing about 200 MeV per fission event
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ The mass defect (Δm) is the difference between the mass of the nucleus and the sum of its individual nucleons. This 'missing mass' is the binding energy holding the nucleus together: E = Δm × c². In U-235 fission, about 0.1% of the mass is converted to energy — a tiny fraction, but c² is so enormous (9×10¹⁶) that 1 kg of U-235 releases energy equivalent to ~2,500 tons of coal!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: B. Nuclear fusion is already used in commercial power plants worldwide, providing cheap, clean energy with no radioactive waste
choices.feedback: 💡 Controlled nuclear fusion has NOT yet been achieved commercially! While fusion works in laboratories (like ITER and NIF), sustaining it long enough to produce net energy for a power grid remains one of the greatest engineering challenges. The extreme temperatures (~100 million °C) and plasma confinement are incredibly difficult. Fusion power is often said to be '30 years away' — scientists hope to achieve commercial fusion by 2050-2060.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Pivoting your strategy when needed is a sign of adaptive thinking.

choices.label: C. The binding energy per nucleon is highest for the lightest elements (hydrogen) and decreases as elements get heavier, which is why hydrogen fusion releases the most energy
choices.feedback: 💡 The binding energy per nucleon is LOWEST for the lightest elements and peaks at iron-56! The curve rises from hydrogen, peaks at iron/nickel, then gradually decreases for heavier elements. Fusion of light elements releases energy because products move UP the curve (toward higher binding energy). Fission of heavy elements also releases energy because products move UP the curve toward iron. Iron is the most stable nucleus.

skill_explanation.resilience: Learning from setbacks rather than giving up shows resilience.

choices.label: D. Radioactive dating can determine the age of any material — from yesterday's newspaper to the oldest rocks — by choosing the right radioactive isotope
choices.feedback: 💡 Each dating method has a specific range! Carbon-14 (half-life 5,730 years) only works for organic materials up to ~50,000 years old. For older rocks, potassium-argon dating (half-life 1.3 billion years) is used. Very recent materials cannot be dated because too little decay has occurred. Also, only materials that originally contained radioactive isotopes can be dated — you can't date a piece of glass with C-14.

skill_explanation.empathy: Understanding the impact on people around you shows care for others.

glossary_terms.definition: An atomic model where electrons orbit the nucleus in fixed energy levels (shells). Electrons can jump between levels by absorbing or emitting specific amounts of energy.
A type of radiation consisting of 2 protons and 2 neutrons (helium nucleus). Highly ionizing but stopped by paper or skin. Emitted during alpha decay.
A high-energy electron emitted from the nucleus during beta decay, when a neutron converts to a proton. Moderately penetrating, stopped by aluminum.
High-energy electromagnetic radiation emitted from the nucleus. No charge, no mass, highly penetrating — requires thick lead or concrete for shielding.
The time taken for half the radioactive atoms in a sample to decay. After n half-lives, the fraction remaining is (1/2)^n. Cannot be changed by physical or chemical means.
The splitting of a heavy nucleus (like U-235) into two lighter nuclei plus neutrons and energy. Used in nuclear reactors and atomic bombs.
The combining of light nuclei (like hydrogen) into heavier nuclei (like helium) with release of enormous energy. Powers the Sun and stars.
Einstein's E = mc². A small amount of mass converts to enormous energy because c² (speed of light squared) is approximately 9 × 10¹⁶ m²/s².
The spontaneous breakdown of unstable nuclei, emitting alpha, beta, or gamma radiation. It is random — you cannot predict which atom will decay next, only the probability.
A self-sustaining nuclear reaction where neutrons from one fission event cause further fissions. Requires critical mass to sustain itself.
Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons. For example, C-12, C-13, and C-14 are all carbon but have 6, 7, and 8 neutrons respectively.
The minimum amount of fissile material needed to sustain a chain reaction. Below this mass, too many neutrons escape without causing further fissions.

endings.title: Nuclear Physicist
endings.message: You have achieved mastery in the Atomic Physics Lab! Your knowledge of atomic structure, radioactivity, and nuclear reactions is extraordinary, matched by exceptional ethical awareness. The visiting nuclear medicine doctor offers to mentor you. Dr. Curie says you embody the best of science — curiosity tempered by responsibility.

endings.title: Skilled Atomic Researcher
endings.message: You have become a skilled atomic physics researcher. Your understanding of decay, half-life, and nuclear reactions is solid. Dr. Curie recommends you for the advanced physics track. Your combination of knowledge and ethical awareness makes you a responsible scientist. Keep exploring!

endings.title: Competent Atomic Physics Student
endings.message: You completed the Atomic Physics Lab with a solid grasp of the fundamentals. Some topics were challenging — especially nuclear equations and half-life calculations — but you persevered. Dr. Curie says your foundation is good and encourages continued study.

endings.title: Struggling Student
endings.message: Atomic physics was a challenging journey. The abstract concepts of radioactive decay and nuclear equations were confusing. But you did not give up! Dr. Curie arranges extra support and says: 'The atom does not reveal its secrets easily. Keep asking questions and the answers will come.'

endings.title: Ethics Under Review
endings.message: Your radiation safety awareness and ethical standing fell below acceptable levels. Dr. Curie has placed you under ethics review — nuclear science carries too much responsibility for careless attitudes. Complete the ethics certification program to demonstrate that you understand the gravity of this field.
